title: Measuring 3D In-vivo Shoulder Kinematics using Biplanar Videoradiography
protocol: Ask the participant to lie supine onto the CT examination table with their arms at their sides.
Position the participant off center on the table such that the entire hemi-torso is available for imaging based on the participant's size.

Acquire scout images ensuring the CT field of view includes the clavicle (superiorly), the distal humeral epicondyles (inferiorly), the entire glenohumeral joint (laterally), and the costovertebral and sternocostal joints (medially).
Acquire the CT scan with parameters: scan mode = helical; tube voltage = 120 kVp; tube current: 200-400 mA (auto); slice thickness = 0.66 mm; FOV = 34 cm.
Verify the scan quality and field of view.
Reformat the acquisition using an image matrix size of 512 x 512 pixels.
Set the camera aperture to the default setting (f/5.6).
Open the camera software and load the study protocol to each camera (sampling rate: 60 Hz, exposure time: 1,100 µs).
Select Vascular setting on both x-ray generator control panels.
Set the exposure time on the pulse generator to 0.25 s.
Hold down the PREP buttons on the control panels.
Simultaneously press and hold the EXPOSE buttons once both screens read Ready to Expose.
Depress the PREP and EXPOSE buttons on both control panels, and simultaneously depress and hold the foot pedal (or hand-held) to trigger x-ray production.
Repeat steps until the x-ray tube's heat unit exceeds the level required by the manufacturer to acquire images.
Verify camera synchronization and image focus.
Place the distortion correction grid on the image intensifier.
Select the Cardiac setting on both x-ray generator control panels.
Initiate the camera acquisition through the camera software and acquire x-ray images.
Preview the resulting images.
Determine the elapsed time from the trigger pulse for each system.
If the difference in elapsed time between cameras exceeds 2 µs, determine which camera is firing late.
Specify a frame delay in the camera software to resolve timing issues.
Visually inspect the sharpness of the image to verify camera focus.
Analyze a profile line drawn across a bead within the distortion correction grid using image processing software.
Inspect the slope of the pixel gray values along this profile line.
If necessary, refocus the cameras and repeat the previous steps.
Position the chair in the biplane imaging volume so that the shoulder to be tested is centered approximately where the biplane x-ray beams intersect.
Ask the participant to be seated in a comfortable upright posture with arms resting at his/her side.
Secure a lead-lined protective vest across the participant's torso to cover their abdomen and the contralateral shoulder and chest.
Turn on the light within the system's x-ray source.
Raise the system until the participant's shadow cast onto the image intensifier is at the level of their axilla.
Gently move the participant on their chair within the biplane image volume while watching their shadow cast onto each image intensifier.
Keep the light source on and ask the participant to perform the motion to be tested.
Ensure that the participant's shoulder remains within the radiographic field of view during the entire motion trial.
Collimate x-ray beams to reduce exposure if possible.
Repeat steps until it appears that the participant's setup within the image volume is appropriate.
Return to the control room to run the x-ray control panels and cameras.
Set the x-ray control panel to low power fluoroscopy mode (60 kVp, 3-4 mA).
Set the pulse generator to a 0.25 s acquisition.
Explain to the participant that an image will be taken so that their position can be verified in the images.
Describe the series of events that will happen to the participant.
Warn the participant about the sounds the system makes (e.g., clicks, hums) to prevent any apprehension.
Don a lead-lined protective vest.
Retrieve the hand-held trigger and move as far away from the x-ray sources as possible to minimize exposure while still maintaining a clear line of sight and communication with the participant.
Stand behind a lead-lined shield with a window if possible.
Start the cameras in the x-ray control room.
Prime the x-ray control panel as described previously (steps 2.2.3-2.2.5).
Notify researcher #2 when the system is ready to expose.
Indicate to the participant about image acquisition.
Trigger the radiographic image acquisition using the hand-held remote trigger.
Inform the participant that an image was taken and excuse yourself to the control room.
Inspect the images in the x-ray control room.
Focus only on the participant's position and the visibility of all bones to be tracked.
Repeat steps 2.4.5-2.4.12 until the participant's position is satisfactory if necessary.
Do not move the x-ray system during the data collection session unless new calibration and distortion correction images are collected for each configuration.
Instruct the participant to move as little as possible for the duration of the data collection session to avoid having to repeat setup procedures.
Set the optimized radiographic technique on the x-ray control panel (based on preliminary testing).
Use a radiographic protocol of 70 kVp, 320 mA, 2 ms, and focal spot = 1.0 mm, with the camera collecting at 60 Hz and an exposure time of 1,100 µs.
Set the pulse generator to 0.25 s.
Inform the participant that the next image will be a formal image acquisition.
Instruct the participant to sit upright with their arm resting at their side.
Acquire an image as previously described.
Inspect the images for brightness and contrast, and visibility of all necessary bones.
Determine if adjustments are needed based on image quality.
Modify radiographic parameters such as f-stop, camera exposure time, kVp, or mA.
Reacquire the static image with modified parameters.
Repeat steps until image quality is acceptable within IRB-approved dose estimates.
Inspect images for technical quality issues (e.g., corrupt frames).
Save trial images from each camera (e.g., "green_still.cine", "red_still.cine").
Maintain radiographic parameters used in the static trial image.
Set pulse generator to a 2.0 s exposure for dynamic image acquisition.
Teach the participant the motion to be performed.
Verify that the chair and clothing do not interfere with shoulder motion.
Practice the motion trial with the participant.
Use the verbal cue "Ready…and…go" paced over 2 seconds.
Retrieve the hand-held remote trigger.
Move to a safe place in the lab with clear line of sight to the participant.
Reset the pulse generator to 2.0 s.
Start the cameras and prime the x-ray control panel.
Notify researcher #2 when the system is ready to expose.
Ask the research participant, "Are you ready?"
Wait for an affirmative response from the participant.
Use the verbal cue "Ready…and…go" paced over 2 seconds.
Manually trigger the x-ray system when the participant initiates arm motion.
Inspect the trial images for quality, including brightness and contrast.
Check the trial images for any corrupt frames.
Save motion trials from each camera.
Repeat steps 2.6.1-2.6.7 to collect all motion trials within the approved radiation safety protocol.
Collect calibration images.
Set the pulse generator to a 0.5 s exposure.
Position the calibration cube in the middle of the imaging volume.
Acquire and save cube images.
Collect images for distortion correction and nonuniformity correction.
Remove all objects from the radiographic field of view.
Set pulse generator to a 0.5 s exposure.
Attach distortion correction grid to green image intensifier surface.
Acquire grid and white-field images.
Save acquired images appropriately.
Move distortion correction grid to red image intensifier.
Repeat steps for acquiring grid and white-field images on red image intensifier.
Modify image filenames as appropriate.
Open an image processing program and import the CT images.
Segment the humerus from the surrounding soft tissues.
Create an extension that connects the anterior aspect of the rib to the manubrium for digitizing the sternocostal joint.
Perform a Boolean operation on the finished mask with a black mask (black minus bone).
Crop the image stack along all three axes to eliminate non-bone pixels.
Leave some black pixels at the edges of this 3D bounding box.
Import the TIFF image stack for the bone to be processed.
Convert the TIFF stack to a .RAW file and render a 3D bone model based on the known pixel dimensions and image spacing using the proprietary software.

Define the geometric center of the humeral head as the coordinates of the optimized sphere's center, which minimizes the distance between the sphere's surface and the humeral articular surface using a least-squares algorithm.
Locate the medial and lateral epicondyles at the widest section of the distal humerus.
Define the root of the scapular spine on the medial border along the scapular spine.
Locate the posterior acromioclavicular joint at the posterior aspect of the clavicular facet on the scapular acromion.
Identify the inferior angle at the inferior-most point on the scapula.
Digitize the undersurface of the acromion lateral to the spine of the scapula for the acromion region.
Define the entire articulating surface of the glenoid as the glenoid region.
Locate the anterior rib at the medial-most portion of the rib extension.
Identify the posterior rib at the superior/inferior midpoint of the posterior aspect of the facet on the head of the rib.
Pinpoint the lateral rib at the lateral-most aspect of the rib when the anterior and posterior rib points are aligned vertically on the screen.
Perform non-uniformity correction: The software averages approximately 30 frames to produce a single high-quality bright-field image.
Use the bright-field image to calculate the true radiographic density along the ray from the x-ray source to each pixel of each frame.
The sum of the radiographic density is proportional to the logarithm of the bright field for that pixel minus the logarithm of the observation image for that pixel (i.e., log-sub processing).
Perform distortion correction: The software averages approximately 30 frames to produce a single image and reduces noise effect in any individual image.

The distortion correction software creates an affine map from each triple of adjacent bead positions in the distortion grid image to the known position of those three beads in the Lucite distortion correction grid.
This collection of small affine maps is used to resample each observed frame of the motion trial into the true coordinates represented by the orthogonal array of beads.
Apply distortion and non-uniformity corrections to all frames of each trial.
Perform image calibration using proprietary software.
Adjust observed calibration object bead locations to their known 3D locations using a nonlinear optimization algorithm.
Register biplanar calibration images against radiographic images of the same bone collected during data collection.
On the first frame of the motion trial, manually rotate and translate the DRR until it matches well with biplane x-ray images.
Save the manual solution after achieving alignment.
Apply the optimization algorithm to determine an optimal solution based on the initial manual solution.
Visually inspect the optimized solution and adjust if necessary.
Repeat steps 3.5.2-3.5.3 until satisfied with the optimized solution.
For every 10th frame across the motion trial, repeat steps 3.5.1-3.5.4.
Perform an optimization to create interpolated preliminary solutions that are subsequently optimized.
Refine the solutions until all frames of the motion trial are tracked well.
Calculate kinematic outcome measures from landmark trajectories using any programming language.
Calculate joint rotations (Euler angles) and positions as primary kinematic outcomes.
Calculate minimum gap, average gap, and weighted-average contact center for proximity statistics.
Aggregate anatomical proximities across the motion trial to include average contact center.
Determine contact path and contact path length during movement.
Use filtered anatomical landmark coordinates to construct a 16-element transformation matrix for each bone relative to the laboratory coordinate system.
Calculate relative kinematics by relating the anatomical coordinate systems between relevant bones.
Extract joint angles and positions using conventional methods.
Extract glenohumeral kinematics using a Z-X'-Y'' rotation sequence.
Extract scapulothoracic kinematics using a Y-Z'-X'' rotation sequence.
Extract humerothoracic kinematics using a Y-Z'-Y'' rotation sequence.
Calculate the smallest gap between the centroids of the nearest-neighbor triangle on the opposite bone.
Calculate the area-weighted mean of the minimum gap using the software.
Define the measurement area as the triangles closest to the opposite bone whose areas sum to 200 mm².
Incorporate this measurement area in the calculation to ensure that only the surface near to the opposite bone is included.
Calculate the point on the ROI surface that minimizes the weighted distance to all other triangles within the measurement area using the software.
Use inverse square weighting for each triangle, calculated as: triangle area / squared distance to nearest-neighbor centroid.
Calculate the average position of the contact center across the motion trial using the software.
Define the contact path by connecting the coordinates of the weighted-average contact center across the motion trial using the software.
Calculate the length of the contact path across the motion trial using the software.
